title: [realtime-v1] Multiplex recoverable realtime traffic over one WebSocket — epic
body:
## Approved behavior specification

This epic preserves the complete approved behavior of source issue #38, inlined here so the epic is self-contained.

### Source behavior: [18/22] WebSocket — one connection, four kinds of traffic

## Context

The generic REST endpoints issue (#37) left `WS /api/sync` as the one open detail of its surface. This issue closes it out: it defines the single WebSocket connection that must carry four different kinds of traffic at once — binary Yjs update frames for page and canvas content (issue #23), invalidations for rows written by some other process (the IMAP sync worker, a heartbeat, an agent, another device), live delivery of `notifications` rows, and agent streams (turn events and token-by-token deltas from the pi-agent-core runtime, issues #30-33).

Procedurally this was decided long ago: the WS server lives in `semprec-api`, the code in `packages/realtime`, and the only source of events is Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY, because processes are not allowed to talk to each other any other way. The governing principle for this whole area: **WS is never the source of truth** — Postgres owns the state and the REST surface serves it; WS is purely a delivery layer, and every stream type must therefore have an explicit, decided-in-advance answer to "what happens if the message is lost" — including the case where the message is lost server-side, before it ever reaches any socket (see the LISTEN-outage section below).

## Task

Implement `WS /api/sync` in `packages/realtime` as the single multiplexed connection per client, carrying all four traffic types, with an implicit per-user broadcast channel, explicit subscriptions only where volume is real, and a deterministic resume path for each stream type separately.

### One connection per client

A client (browser tab, iOS app, macOS app) holds exactly one WS connection, and all four kinds of traffic are multiplexed over it — there is no separate "Yjs socket" next to a "notification socket". The reason isn't aesthetics: every extra connection is its own heartbeat, its own reconnect state machine, its own place where auth can drift out of sync with the others, and on iOS its own wake-on-foreground handling. More tabs mean more connections (each tab is an independent client with its own displayed state) — the schema doesn't cap that, the same way concurrent sessions aren't capped elsewhere. `semprec-api` holds one LISTEN connection into Postgres per process and fans out to individual sockets in memory — never one LISTEN per client.

**Auth at HTTP upgrade** — session cookie for web, Bearer header for native apps, no post-connect "auth message":

The WS handshake is a plain HTTP request, so it authenticates exactly the way the rest of the API already does (issue #37) — no third path. Web: the browser sends the `httpOnly` session cookie automatically with the upgrade request (same-origin; browsers can't set an `Authorization` header on a WS connection, but they don't need to — the cookie is already there). Native iOS/macOS: the `URLSession` WebSocket task can set headers, so it sends the same `Authorization: Bearer` token from the Keychain used for every REST call. Both paths are verified by the same code against the same `sessions` table; an invalid session means the upgrade ends in a 401 and **no socket is ever created**.

The rejected alternative — a token sent in an initial WS message — only makes sense for clients that can set neither a cookie nor a header; no such client exists in this system. And it isn't free: it creates a "connected but not yet authenticated" state that would need its own timeout, its own cap on how many such connections are allowed, and its own handling of messages arriving before verification. Authenticating at upgrade means an authenticated socket either exists or it doesn't — no in-between state to guard, the same "absence, not runtime gating" logic used elsewhere in the auth model.

Revoking a session mid-connection: the choke-point that sets `sessions.revoked_at` sends a NOTIFY with `session_id`, and `semprec-api` immediately closes every socket of that session (close code 4401) — the same "revocation propagates immediately, never asynchronously" discipline used for push subscriptions. Periodic session re-validation on every ping (below) is only a safety net for a lost NOTIFY, not the primary mechanism.

### Subscription model

**Implicit user channel, explicit subscribe only where volume is real:**

Semprec is a one- to two-user system — the volume of invalidations is the sum of one person's writes, their heartbeats, and sync workers: tens of events per minute at peak, not thousands per second. At this scale, subscription bookkeeping ("this client is subscribed to these databases/views") is pure overhead with its own failure mode: a forgotten unsubscribe, a filter that drifts out of sync with what the client actually shows — and every such bug means **silently stale UI**, exactly the nondeterminism the project has ruled out. Broadcasting all thin invalidations (below) to every socket of the user has no silent failure mode inside the connection — the client discards what it isn't displaying, and the cost is bytes, not correctness.

Explicit subscribe exists only where volume or payload size is real:
- Binary Yjs updates flow only for documents the client has announced via `doc:open` (and ended via `doc:close`) — streaming every update of every document to every client would be real volume with no consumer.
- Token-by-token deltas of an agent run flow only to clients that sent `agent:watch` for a specific `runId` — a high-frequency stream watched by at most one screen.
- Turn-level agent events (run status change, completed turn), by contrast, go over the implicit channel to everyone — they're thin, and an "agent finished" badge makes sense on every device.

**Rejected: fine-grained subscriptions on databases/items/views.** This is the pattern from multi-tenant collaborative tools (Notion-scale), which solves two problems that don't exist here: the event volume of other users, and per-subscriber permission filtering. Here the server would have to evaluate, for every event, which subscriptions it matches — either a second, parallel filter engine alongside the view/filter compiler, or per-event evaluation in the hot path — for a payoff of saving a few kilobytes per minute. If real sharing arrives later (`resource_grants`), a subscription layer would be built on top of whatever permission enforcement exists then; designing it now would mean guessing the shape of an enforcement layer that deliberately doesn't exist yet.

### Message catalog — protocol v1

```
# client → server (JSON text frame)
{ "type": "doc:open",      "docId": "…" }                -- start sending me updates for this doc + start Yjs sync
{ "type": "doc:close",     "docId": "…" }
{ "type": "agent:watch",   "runId": "…", "afterEventId": 123 }   -- replay persisted events after the cursor, then live
{ "type": "agent:unwatch", "runId": "…" }

# server → client (JSON text frame)
{ "type": "invalidate", "scope": "item",   "databaseId": "…", "itemId": "…",
  "op": "create"|"update"|"delete", "updatedAt": "…" }   -- row changed; updatedAt = ifVersion token (issue #37)
{ "type": "invalidate", "scope": "schema", "databaseId": "…" }   -- database properties/views/definition changed
{ "type": "notification", "notification": { … } }        -- full notifications row (exception noted below)
{ "type": "agent:event",  "runId": "…", "eventId": 124, "kind": "turn_end", "payload": { … } }
{ "type": "agent:delta",  "runId": "…", "delta": "…" }   -- ephemeral token stream, watched runs only

# binary frames (either direction)
16 B docId (uuid) + y-protocols sync message (SyncStep1 / SyncStep2 / Update)
```

**Invalidations are thin references — "X changed, refetch if your version is older", never data.** The REST endpoints layer (issue #37) already decided that every write returns the authoritative row state and that the REST surface is the only place `owner`/`computed`/trash semantics get enforced during serialization. Sending full rows over WS would create a **second serialization path** — every future field-level rule would have to be enforced twice, and the two paths drifting apart is exactly the silent drift the choke-point exists to prevent. A thin invalidation has no such surface: it carries only identifiers, the operation, and `updatedAt` — the same version token issue #37 uses as `ifVersion`. The client compares it to what's in its cache: a match means "already current, do nothing" (a client's own writes echo back harmlessly this way, since the REST response already delivered the authoritative state); an older value means refetch through the existing `GET`/`query` surface. A deterministic decision from two numbers, no heuristics.

The key property for consistency: a lost thin invalidation is **fully recoverable** — the client has an at-most-slightly-stale cache that the next invalidation or reconnect refetch (below) will correct, and an offline-first client must already be able to reconcile via REST and `ifVersion`/409 anyway. WS therefore optimizes latency, never carries correctness — the same division of labor as "the only synchronization guarantee is REST; WS just delivers the in-between changes."

**Rejected: full row in the push message ("saves a second request").** Attractive at first glance, wrong three times over on the second: (1) a second serialization path alongside the REST choke-point, as above; (2) ordering — a push carrying a row could arrive before or after the same client's own REST response, and the client would have to decide which representation wins, whereas with a thin invalidation the answer is always "whatever refetch returns is authoritative"; (3) the NOTIFY payload limit of 8000 bytes (below) would force an indirection through a table for larger rows anyway — the complexity would land exactly where it promised savings. The saved request is also often zero anyway: thanks to `updatedAt` in the thin event, the client only refetches what's actually stale.

**Yjs frames** don't invent their own encoding — they use the existing `y-protocols/sync` format (the same small MIT family as `yjs` itself, issue #23): `SyncStep1` (client sends its state vector), `SyncStep2` (server responds with a diff), `Update` (ongoing changes in either direction). The server side is handled by the same headless `Y.Doc` mechanism issue #23 introduced for agent access (`doc_snapshots.state_vector` + append-only `doc_updates`); an incoming `Update` from a client is written as a new `doc_updates` row (with `created_by` set from the session's origin) and fanned out to other clients with the doc open. Binary, not base64-in-JSON — Yjs updates are the largest-volume payload on the channel, and base64 would mean ~33% overhead plus double re-encoding on both sides; a 16-byte `docId` prefix is enough to demultiplex, the message type itself is carried in the y-protocols varint.

**Notifications are the one message that carries a full row** — a deliberate exception to the "thin" rule, and safe for the same reason the notifications table (issue #37 area) was designed the way it was: `notifications.title` is "finished text, not a template rendered on read", a read model with no enforcement layer for a second serialization path to drift against. Losing a notification message heals exactly the way already decided elsewhere — the client fetches unread rows once on connect, WS just adds live delivery on top.

### Event source — LISTEN/NOTIFY, references instead of payloads

The only permitted transport between `semprec-agents`/`semprec-mailsync@*` and the WS server in `semprec-api` is Postgres NOTIFY — no direct RPC, because processes are only allowed to talk through Postgres. Postgres caps NOTIFY payloads at 8000 bytes; instead of working around that (chunking, compression), the limit is promoted to a discipline: NOTIFY on the `semprec_events` channel always carries only `kind` + identifiers + `updatedAt` (on the order of 200 bytes), never content. A binary Yjs update can't go over NOTIFY even in principle — the event carries `{ docId, updateId }`, and `semprec-api` fetches the bytea from `doc_updates` with a single primary-key SELECT before fan-out. Emitting NOTIFY is the responsibility of the same write paths that already exist: the choke-point after writes to `items`/`databases`/`properties`/`views`, the `doc_updates` write path, inserts into `notifications` — no trigger, no polling, the same "second write next to the first" pattern used for notifications.

NOTIFY is transactional — delivered only on commit, never for a rolled-back transaction. That isn't a limitation but a guarantee for free: an invalidation can never arrive ahead of the state it announces, and there's no "event for a write that didn't happen" — determinism that a side-channel transport (Redis pub/sub and the like) would have to painstakingly reconstruct.

**The one exception where NOTIFY carries content instead of a reference**: token-by-token deltas of agent runs, on their own channel `semprec_agent_stream`. Writing every delta to a table would be write amplification with no audit value — the audit trail is turn-level, in `agent_run_events` (see below); a delta is purely a display stream, and losing one is immediately healed by the persistent turn event carrying the final message text. The emitter in `semprec-agents` splits any delta longer than ~7500 bytes across multiple NOTIFYs — a mechanical safety margin against the limit, not the normal case.

### Table `agent_run_events`

The pi-agent-core issues (#30-33) read and write this log in three places (reconstructing sleeping conversations from `initialState.messages`, a startup sweep appending a synthetic `tool_result`, turn-by-turn streaming); the table itself is **created authoritatively by issue #30**, which also writes the turn-level events into it as runs execute. This issue consumes and extends it — its shape matters here because it is dictated by resume: `id` is both the `afterEventId` cursor used in the `watch` message and the ordering for the `Entry[]` reconstruction those issues rely on. The DDL below is kept as reference only; the migration lives in #30.

```sql
CREATE TABLE agent_run_events (
  id bigserial PRIMARY KEY,                 -- monotonic cursor: resume and Entry[] reconstruction ordering
  agent_run_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES agent_runs(id),
  kind text NOT NULL,                       -- 'turn_start' | 'message' | 'tool_use' | 'tool_result' | 'turn_end' | 'run_status'
  payload jsonb NOT NULL,                   -- full message (AgentMessage shape) -- source for reconstruction, not just display
  at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX agent_run_events_run_idx ON agent_run_events (agent_run_id, id);
```

The persistent-vs-ephemeral split is taken directly from the pi event mapping in those issues: turn-level events (`turn_start`, completed messages, `tool_use`/`tool_result`, `turn_end`, run status changes) are written by `semprec-agents` into `agent_run_events`, and a thin NOTIFY is emitted after commit; `message_update` deltas go **only** over the `semprec_agent_stream` channel, never into the table. A client watching a run sends `agent:watch` with the last known `eventId` — the server replays `SELECT … WHERE agent_run_id = $1 AND id > $2 ORDER BY id` and then switches to the live stream. Deltas lost between an outage and resume are not replayed — and don't need to be: the final text of each turn arrives as a persistent `message` event, so the only thing an outage costs is the on-screen typing effect, not information.

### Resume after an outage — every stream its own path, no universal cursor

| Stream | Resume mechanism |
|---|---|
| Yjs docs | own state-vector sync — after reconnect the client sends `SyncStep1` for each open doc and gets exactly the missing diff; CRDT commutativity/idempotence make a duplicate delivered update a no-op. The strongest resume in the whole protocol, and free from the format itself, no cursor on our side |
| Agent stream | `agent_run_events.id` as the cursor in `agent:watch` — persistent events are replayed from the log, ephemeral deltas deliberately are not |
| Invalidations | no cursor — reconnect means refetching what the client displays, see the decision below |
| Notifications | one-time fetch of unread rows (`read_at IS NULL`) on connect — unchanged from what was already decided for notifications |

**Chosen: invalidations after reconnect — a deliberate refetch of active views and open items, not an event log with a cursor.** After an outage the client doesn't need "every event that happened in between" — it needs a fresh state of whatever is on screen. And the existing REST surface already does exactly that: re-run the query for active views (keyset, bounded) and `GET` the open item/doc. The work is bounded by what the client displays (a handful of views plus one item plus open docs), not by the length of the outage — a refetch after a week offline costs the same as after a second. The client holds a single "connection was interrupted" flag and, on reconnect, does the refetch before it starts trusting new invalidations — a deterministic two-state protocol, no time windows or heuristics.

**Rejected: a persistent invalidation log with a client-side cursor.** The event-sourcing answer (a change table, the client keeps a position, replays on reconnect) would mean: a second persistent event infrastructure alongside `agent_run_events`, a retention/pruning job, per-client cursor persistence, and an ordering guarantee across all write sources — and its one consumer would still end up doing a refetch after replay, since thin events don't carry data (decided above). For a single-user system with a handful of clients, where reconnect is rare and refetch is cheap, that's infrastructure for a scale that doesn't exist. It's addable later if refetch-after-outage becomes a measured problem — the protocol shape wouldn't change, `invalidate` events would just get an id and the client a new resume mode.

### Server-side LISTEN loss is not an exception to the governing principle

NOTIFY only delivers to connections that are actually listening at the moment of commit — when `semprec-api`'s single LISTEN connection drops and reconnects (a Postgres restart, an unattended upgrade, a connection reset), every event committed in that gap is irrecoverably gone, while WS clients stay happily connected and nothing would force them through the resume paths — exactly the silently stale UI this area rules out, just one layer down. The answer is as blunt as the backpressure answer below: on loss and re-establishment of the LISTEN connection (and symmetrically on a controlled process shutdown), the server closes **all** WS sockets with close code 1012 ("Service Restart") — every client is thereby forced through its resume path (state-vector sync, `agent:watch` cursor, refetch of what's displayed, unread fetch), and the gap in the event stream heals deterministically, not by luck on the next invalidation of the same row. A considered alternative — the server "replaying what was missed" once LISTEN is restored — has nothing to replay from: NOTIFY is never persisted, and a persistent event log was rejected above; anything short of a full disconnect would be a heuristic over an unknown-sized hole. A mass 1012 is blunt but correct, and the event is rare (a Postgres restart, a deploy) — the cost is one reconnect+refetch for a handful of clients, not an operating mode.

### Heartbeat, limits, backpressure

Dead connections are detected by the server via protocol-level WS ping/pong (RFC 6455 control frames, not an application message — both the browser and `URLSession` answer these on their own, no client code needed): a ping every 30 seconds, no pong before the next ping closes the connection (~90 s detection window). In the same tick the server re-validates the session against `sessions` — a safety net for the immediate NOTIFY-based revocation above. After a drop, the client reconnects with exponential backoff plus jitter (1 s up to a 30 s ceiling), and on successful reconnect walks the resume paths above — reconnect is a normal operating state (phone in a tunnel, laptop waking up), not an exception.

Limits for v1, deliberately few numbers: max client frame size 2 MB — a Yjs update from ordinary editing is much smaller, and large binary assets don't belong in a doc anyway (images and files live in blob storage, referenced from the doc, not embedded); a max of 32 open `doc:open` subscriptions per connection (no UI shows more open documents than that at once). The number of connections per session is not capped — more tabs is legitimate, and a session cap wouldn't solve anything auth doesn't already solve.

**Chosen: slow consumer — coalesce invalidations, then disconnect; never unbounded buffers, never per-type drop logic.** Invalidations are idempotent hints, so the per-socket outgoing queue coalesces them by (`databaseId`, `itemId`) — if two invalidations for the same row are pending, only the one with the newer `updatedAt` survives. That alone keeps the queue small under any realistic load. When a socket's `bufferedAmount` still exceeds 4 MB anyway (the client genuinely isn't reading — a frozen tab, a dead link the ping hasn't caught yet), the server closes the connection with close code 1013 ("try again later") instead of accumulating memory.

Why disconnect is the right answer, not per-type dropping from the buffer: every stream type already has a reliable resume path from the decisions above — Yjs state vector, `agent_run_events` cursor, reconnect refetch, unread fetch. A disconnected client therefore walks exactly the path that guarantees end-to-end consistency anyway, whereas selectively dropping messages inside a live connection would create a new, untested in-between state ("connected, but with holes in the stream") for a scale of 1-2 clients that will never actually exercise it. The resume paths were designed first precisely so that backpressure — and the LISTEN outage above — could have an answer this simple.

## Scope

### In scope

- The `WS /api/sync` endpoint in `packages/realtime` (`semprec-api`): HTTP upgrade with auth against the `sessions` table (cookie/Bearer), 401 on an invalid session.
- One LISTEN connection into Postgres per `semprec-api` process, fan-out to sockets in memory.
- Handling every message in the catalog (`doc:open`, `doc:close`, `agent:watch`, `agent:unwatch` inbound; `invalidate`, `notification`, `agent:event`, `agent:delta`, plus binary Yjs frames, outbound).
- Emitting NOTIFY on the `semprec_events` channel (references) and `semprec_agent_stream` channel (deltas) from the write choke-points that already exist (issue #37, issue #23, the agent-runtime issues).
- Consuming the `agent_run_events` table created in issue #30 (the table, its index, and the turn-level writes exist from there): the `agent:watch` replay via the `id` cursor, the live fan-out, and the thin NOTIFY emission after commit that this delivery layer adds.
- Binary Yjs sync (SyncStep1/SyncStep2/Update) wired to `doc_snapshots`/`doc_updates` from issue #23.
- Session revocation triggering immediate socket closure (close code 4401).
- Resume logic for all four streams (state-vector sync, `agent_run_events` cursor, invalidation refetch flag, unread-notifications fetch).
- Mass close with code 1012 on loss/re-establishment of the LISTEN connection, or on a controlled shutdown.
- Heartbeat ping/pong, client-side reconnect backoff, frame/subscription limits, invalidation coalescing, and backpressure close with code 1013.

### Out of scope

- Observability of the WS layer (connection metrics, stream logging, alerting on LISTEN outages) — that is issue #39 (Observability), an explicit follow-up outside this scope.
- Fine-grained subscriptions at the database/item/view level (considered and rejected — see the Event source section above; would be built on top of future `resource_grants` sharing, if that ever arrives).
- Carrying full rows in invalidation messages (rejected — a second serialization path).
- A persistent invalidation event log with a client-side cursor (rejected — infrastructure for a scale that doesn't exist; addable later).
- Anything that belongs to issue #23 (the Yjs/blocks binary format and CRDT logic itself) or issues #30-33 (the agent runtime, generating the actual `agent:event`/`agent:delta` content) — this issue only defines how that content is delivered over WS, not how it's produced.

## Dependencies

**Depends on:** #23, #30, #37

- **Issue #37 (Generic endpoints over the choke-point)**: WS invalidations carry the same `updatedAt`/`ifVersion` token that the REST surface returns and enforces as the authoritative source of truth — WS is purely a delivery layer over that surface, and every refetch (after an invalidation or after resume) goes through the existing GET/query endpoints. Auth at WS upgrade uses the same `sessions` table and the same revocation discipline as REST.
- **Issue #23 (Blocks and canvas on Yjs CRDT)**: binary Yjs sync in `WS /api/sync` is a direct continuation — it uses the same headless `Y.Doc` mechanism, the `doc_snapshots.state_vector` and `doc_updates` tables, the same `y-protocols/sync` format, and the same CRDT commutativity/idempotence that Yjs-stream resume relies on.
- **Issues #30-33 (pi-agent-core)**: this issue supplies the missing transport layer for the agent stream that the pi-agent-core runtime already produces (turn events, token deltas, `initialState.messages` reconstruction). The `agent_run_events` table itself is created and written by issue #30; this issue builds the WS delivery on top of it and defines the exact cursor (`id`/`afterEventId`) and the persistent (`agent_run_events` + NOTIFY) vs. ephemeral (`semprec_agent_stream` only) split of the stream.

## Reference to the specification

Source: `vize/backend.html`, lines 5702-6080 — the section "One connection, four kinds of traffic — and none of them makes WS a second source of truth." Contains the full text of the decisions "Auth at HTTP upgrade", "Invalidation and notification without subscriptions" (plus the rejected "Fine-grained subscriptions on databases/items/views"), "Invalidations are thin references" (plus the rejected "Full row in the push message"), "NOTIFY carries only identifiers", the `agent_run_events` table definition, "Invalidations after reconnect" (plus the rejected "Persistent invalidation log with a client cursor"), the server-side LISTEN-loss discussion, and "Slow consumer — coalesce invalidations, then disconnect."

## Decisions

- Authentication? Cookie/Bearer at HTTP upgrade; no half-authenticated socket state.
- Invalidations? References plus REST refetch, because WS must not duplicate authoritative serialization.
- Resume? Stream-specific mechanisms, because no universal cursor represents CRDT, events, cache, and unread state correctly.
- LISTEN outage? Close all sockets with 1012, because missing NOTIFY events cannot be replayed.

## Out of scope

- Fine-grained row subscriptions, full-row invalidations, a persistent invalidation log, presence/Awareness, and observability of this layer.

## Checklist

- [ ] #160 — Establish the authenticated multiplexed WebSocket lifecycle
- [ ] #161 — Bridge transactional invalidations and notifications through PostgreSQL
- [ ] #162 — Synchronize open Yjs documents with state-vector recovery
- [ ] #163 — Replay and stream watched agent runs
- [ ] #242 — Enforce server-side limits, LISTEN-outage closure, coalescing, and backpressure
- [ ] #164 — Implement client reconnect with jitter and per-stream recovery
